title: Demonstrate an understanding of feedlot feed ingredient and blends

lessons.title: The nutrients cattle need
lessons.html:
Why ingredients matter

A feedlot ration is a recipe. Each ingredient brings certain nutrients, and the nutritionist combines them so that cattle grow fast and stay healthy at the lowest cost. If you understand what each ingredient does, you will understand why mixing errors are dangerous and why you must report poor ingredients.

The main nutrients

  • Energy – the fuel for growth and fattening. Grains such as maize give most of the energy.
  • Protein – needed to build muscle. Comes from oilcakes and from non-protein nitrogen such as urea, which rumen microbes turn into protein.
  • Fibre (roughage) – keeps the rumen working, makes cattle chew and produce saliva, which buffers acid.
  • Minerals and vitamins – calcium, phosphorus, salt, trace minerals and vitamins for bones, health and growth.
  • Water – the most important nutrient of all.

The rumen

Cattle are ruminants. Their rumen is a large fermentation tank full of microbes that break down feed. The microbes need a steady supply of feed. A sudden change from roughage to lots of grain makes the rumen produce acid quickly, causing acidosis: cattle go off feed, have loose dung, become lame and can die. This is why feedlots change rations step by step and why the right amount of roughage in each blend is essential.

Dry matter

Ingredients contain different amounts of water. Silage may be mostly water, while maize grain is mostly dry matter. Rations are formulated on a dry matter basis, so a change in silage moisture after rain changes what the cattle actually get. Report wet or changed ingredients to the supervisor.

lessons.title: Common feedlot ingredients
lessons.html:
Know your ingredients

GroupExamplesMain role
EnergyMaize meal, flaked or rolled maize, hominy chop, wheat branFast growth and fattening
RoughageLucerne hay, grass hay, maize or sorghum silage, maize stoverRumen health, chewing
ProteinSunflower oilcake, soybean oilcake, cottonseed oilcake, brewers grainMuscle growth
Non-protein nitrogenFeed-grade ureaCheap nitrogen for rumen microbes
Liquid feedsMolassesPalatability, binds dust, some energy
PremixMinerals, vitamins, salt, buffers, registered additivesBalanced nutrition, health

Quality checks on ingredients

  • Grain – dry, free of mould, insects, stones and foreign matter. Mouldy grain may contain mycotoxins that harm cattle.
  • Hay – green or good colour, leafy, no mould, no dust, no wire or plastic.
  • Silage – sweet, sour smell; reject black, slimy, hot or mouldy silage.
  • Oilcakes – no lumps, mould or off smells.
  • Molasses – not watered down or fermenting.

Dangerous ingredients

Urea is toxic if too much is eaten or it is not well mixed. Cattle can die quickly of urea poisoning. Never add more than the ration sheet says and make sure it is mixed evenly. Ionophores and some other additives are toxic to horses and donkeys. Store premixes and additives in a locked, dry store and follow the label and the nutritionist. Wear gloves and a dust mask when handling premix.

lessons.title: Blends and rations through the feeding period
lessons.html:
From starter to finisher

Cattle arriving at the feedlot have mostly eaten veld grass. Their rumen must adapt slowly to grain. The feedlot uses a series of blends:

  1. Starter ration – high in roughage, lower in grain, palatable to get new cattle eating. Often fed with good hay for the first days.
  2. Grower or intermediate ration – less roughage, more grain, as cattle adapt.
  3. Finisher ration – high in grain and energy, with just enough roughage for rumen health, to put on fat cover before slaughter.

The number of days on each ration is set by the nutritionist. Moving cattle too fast up the steps causes acidosis and bloat.

Making a good blend

  • Each ingredient must be weighed exactly according to the ration sheet.
  • Ingredients must be loaded in the set order and mixed for the set time, so every mouthful has the same nutrients.
  • A poorly mixed ration lets cattle pick out the grain or get too much urea or premix in one place.
  • Feed must be fresh; mixed rations with silage can heat and spoil if left too long.

Checking the blend

Look at the mixed feed: it should be even in colour and texture with no balls of hay or pockets of meal. The feedlot may send samples to a laboratory to check that the blend matches the formula. Keep records of every batch mixed.

Key points

  • Rations combine energy, protein, roughage, minerals and water.
  • Roughage keeps the rumen healthy; too much grain too fast causes acidosis.
  • Check every ingredient for mould, moisture and foreign matter.
  • Urea and some additives are toxic; never exceed the ration sheet.
  • Cattle move from starter to grower to finisher blends step by step.
